nameStory: The 'definite' tussock moth gets its name from the clear, well-defined markings on the male's wings that distinguish it from its fuzzy-looking relatives. The 'tussock' part refers to the caterpillar's distinctive tufts of hair that stick out like little bristle brushes, resembling the grass tussocks you might find in a meadow.
description: The Definite Tussock Moth is a small, brownish moth where only the males can fly—females are completely wingless! Males have a wingspan of about 30mm (roughly the size of a large coin), while the flightless females look more like fuzzy, egg-laying machines. You're most likely to spot the hairy, colorful caterpillars rather than the adult moths, as they're much more conspicuous as they munch on leaves of common trees and shrubs.

idTips.label: Wingless Females
idTips.description: Adult females look like gray-brown, fuzzy blobs with no wings at all—they stay put on tree bark and wait for males to find them

idTips.label: Male Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Flying males have brownish wings with distinct white and dark markings that create clear, sharp patterns rather than blurred or fuzzy designs

idTips.label: Caterpillar Tufts
idTips.description: Larvae have distinctive tufts of bristly hairs sticking out from their backs like tiny bottle brushes—soft to look at but don't touch, as they can cause skin irritation

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Males are quite small with wings spanning about the width of a quarter, making them easy to overlook when they flutter around lights

idTips.label: Feeding Damage
idTips.description: Look for chewed leaves on willows, oaks, and maples where the hairy caterpillars have been feeding in irregular patches

habitat: Found throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests, especially where oaks, maples, willows, and birches grow. You'll spot them in suburban yards with mature shade trees, along woodland edges, and in parks where their host trees are common. They prefer areas with a mix of tree species rather than pure coniferous forests.

seasonality.spring: Caterpillars emerge and begin feeding on fresh young leaves of host trees. This is when you're most likely to spot the distinctive hairy larvae.
seasonality.summer: Peak caterpillar activity continues with feeding damage visible on leaves. Adult moths emerge later in summer for mating.
seasonality.fall: Adults are active for mating and egg-laying. Wingless females can be found on tree bark waiting for males.
seasonality.winter: Eggs overwinter on tree bark and branches. No visible activity above ground during cold months.

funFact: Female Definite Tussock Moths are such dedicated mothers that they never leave the spot where they emerged as adults—they live their entire adult lives as wingless, stationary baby-making factories, covering their eggs with their own body hair for protection!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the White-marked Tussock Moth, but the Definite Tussock Moth's male has more clearly defined wing markings (hence 'definite') rather than the blurrier patterns of its white-marked cousin. Memory trick: 'Definite' means you can definitely see the clear wing patterns.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'tussock' moths, these insects aren't actually found in grass tussocks—the name refers to their caterpillars' tufted appearance. The family was recently moved from Lymantriidae to Erebidae, so you might see different family names in older field guides.
compareHints: Compared to the White-marked Tussock Moth in the same genus, the Definite Tussock Moth has sharper, more contrasted wing markings in males and tends to be slightly smaller overall. The caterpillars of both species look very similar with their distinctive hair tufts, but the Definite's adult wing patterns are more clearly defined with stronger contrast between light and dark areas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The closely related Definite Tussock Moth caterpillar looks very similar but lacks the bright white spots that give the White-marked Tussock Moth its name.
